item.text:
**7B.6 Research Note: Abdel Fattah el-Sisi in 2024**

Bottom line: I found **strong evidence against meaningful tolerance of independent investigation**. The clearest pattern is retaliation against journalists, opposition figures, NGO workers, and corruption-related scrutiny. There is some limited positive evidence, mainly the closure of Case 173 and partial lifting of travel bans, plus a few administrative accountability actions, but nothing that shows real tolerance for probing Sisi’s own conduct, assets, campaign finance, or hidden decisions.

| Title | Publisher | Date | URL | Claim-level summary | QIDs |
|---|---|---:|---|---|---|
| Egypt: Spate of Free Speech Prosecutions | Human Rights Watch | 2024-08-29 | https://www.hrw.org/news/2024/08/29/egypt-spate-free-speech-prosecutions | HRW says Egyptian authorities detained and prosecuted critics, including journalists and a researcher, with incommunicado detention, abusive pretrial detention, and terrorism-related charges. It specifically says one case stemmed from reporting on a corruption investigation involving senior pro-Sisi party members, which is direct evidence against tolerance of independent scrutiny. | 7B.6, 7B.2 |
| World Report 2024: Egypt | Human Rights Watch | 2024 | https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2024/country-chapters/egypt | HRW says prosecutors referred three Mada Masr journalists to trial over reporting tied to an unannounced corruption investigation into senior party members, and that civic space remained severely curtailed with asset freezes and travel bans. This is strong evidence that investigative reporting and scrutiny of associates were punished, not tolerated. | 7B.6, 7B.4, 7B.2 |
| Egypt: Court Punishes Activists for Challenging al-Sisi | Human Rights Watch | 2024-02-08 | https://www.hrw.org/news/2024/02/08/egypt-court-punishes-activists-challenging-al-sisi | HRW says Tantawy and supporters were sentenced after peaceful political activism, and that the authorities’ arrests and prosecutions were meant to deter challenge to Sisi. While this is more about political challenge than corruption investigation, it shows a hostile environment for independent inquiry into the ruler’s conduct. | 7B.6, 7B.2 |
| Egypt: Lift travel bans imposed on two human rights lawyers | Amnesty International | 2024-07-09 | https://www.amnesty.org/en/latest/news/2024/07/egypt-lift-travel-bans-imposed-on-two-human-rights-lawyers/ | Amnesty says the authorities announced closure of Case 173 in March 2024 after 13 years, and that travel bans had been lifted for many NGO workers, but not for all. This is the clearest limited positive evidence that some scrutiny-related pressure eased, though it remained partial and reversible. | 7B.6 |
| Egypt: Civic Space Under Siege | Human Rights Watch | 2024-01-11 | https://www.hrw.org/news/2024/01/11/egypt-civic-space-under-siege | HRW says authorities drastically curtailed free expression and assembly before the presidential vote, and that independent organizations faced judicial and security harassment. This undercuts any claim that Sisi tolerated probing journalism or civic oversight around the election environment. | 7B.6, 7B.2 |
| Sisi Government's Repression Taints Egypt-EU Investment Conference | Human Rights Watch | 2024-06-28 | https://www.hrw.org/news/2024/06/28/sisi-governments-repression-taints-egypt-eu-investment-conference | HRW says abuses and repression were fueling Egypt’s economic crisis, and that rights reforms were being sought by external partners because domestic scrutiny remained constrained. This supports the view that the regime was still managing image and access, not welcoming independent examination. | 7B.6, 7B.4 |
| Administrative Control Authority: Major General Amr Adel Named Chairman | Administrative Control Authority | 2024 | https://aca.gov.eg/News/3143.aspx | The ACA announced Sisi’s appointment of Major General Amr Adel as chairman, presenting the body as an oversight institution. This is a weak positive only: it shows formal anti-corruption staffing, but not independent scrutiny of Sisi or protection for investigators probing the presidency. | 7B.6, 7B.4 |
| About the ACA | Administrative Control Authority | 2024 | https://aca.gov.eg/News/2090.aspx | The ACA describes itself as an independent oversight body with legal, financial, and administrative independence and a mandate to combat corruption. This is official self-presentation, useful as a formal-positive claim, but it does not establish real tolerance for scrutiny of presidential conduct or hidden decisions. | 7B.6 |
| Madbouly and accountability authority head discuss enhancing governance and int’l coop | SIS | 2024-08-12 | https://sis.gov.eg/en/media-center/news/madbouly-and-accountability-authority-head-discuss-enhancing-governance-and-int-l-coop/ | The presidency formalized new ACA leadership and discussed governance and cooperation, which suggests some ongoing anti-corruption machinery. But the source is official and does not show autonomy from the presidency, so it is only a limited positive signal. | 7B.6, 7B.4 |

### Search gap

- I did **not** find reliable 2024 evidence that Sisi tolerated independent investigation into his own assets, campaign finance, private associates, or concealed presidential decisions.
- The best available material is mostly about **investigation of critics, NGOs, and journalists**, not open scrutiny of the ruler himself.
- The limited positive items are institutional or administrative, not proof of genuine tolerance.

### Bottom line

- **Strong negative evidence dominates**: independent investigators, journalists, and activists were prosecuted or constrained.
- **Partial positives exist**: Case 173 was closed and some travel bans were lifted, and the ACA kept functioning on paper.
- Overall, 2024 looks **clearly negative** for 7B.6.
